 'Angry Trump' Sentiment Outshines 'Shy Trump' in Midterms
 Lee Gang 
 Seoul 
 Published 
 2026.11.04 13:50 
 View 
 View Count 
 Enlarge image 
 ▲ U.S. President Donald Trump 
 As the opposition Democratic Party in the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 goes beyond reclaiming the House of Representatives and eyes winning the Senate, analyses suggest that the "Shy Trump" phenomenon—which consistently upended poll predictions in past presidential elections—did not appear this time. 
 Observers note that rather than President Donald Trump's hidden supporters, who are rarely captured in polls but rally during actual voting, the sentiments of voters who openly expressed dissatisfaction with President Trump ended up swaying the election results. 
 As of 10:30 p.m. on the 3rd (EST) with vote counting underway, networks including CNN and NBC projected that the Democratic Party would secure a majority in the House of Representatives. 
 According to the Associated Press, the Democrats are projected to reclaim Senate seats in South Carolina and North Carolina previously held by Republicans, and are maintaining an advantage over Republicans in key Senate battlegrounds such as Texas and Kansas. 
 U.S. election forecasting site Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected a 100% probability of the Democrats reclaiming a House majority and a greater than 90% chance of a Democratic victory in the Senate. 
 This largely aligns with the Democratic advantage shown in various pre-election polls. 
 In past U.S. elections, attention has focused on the "Shy Trump" phenomenon, where Trump supporters who are reluctant to respond to polls or reveal their political leanings lend him strength in actual voting. 
 During the 2016, 2020, and 2024 presidential elections, polls underestimated President Trump's support while actual voting yielded higher-than-expected vote shares, making "Shy Trump" a representative variable in election forecasting. 
 However, this midterm election differs from past contests in that backlash and disappointment toward the second Trump administration clearly emerged as a driving force for voter turnout. 
 In fact, according to exit polls of voters conducted by pollster SSRS at the request of major broadcasters, 43% of respondents said they voted to express opposition to President Trump, while only 16% said they voted to express support. 
 Thirty-nine percent of respondents cited the "economy" as the most important issue facing the United States, while 32% chose the "state of democracy." 
 Additionally, 54% of respondents said "government corruption" had a decisive impact on their voting decision, and 49% cited the "cost of living." 
 This suggests that economic hardship and dissatisfaction with government operations, combined with antipathy toward President Trump, may have served as the driving force drawing voters to the polls. 
 At the same time, because President Trump's name was not on the ballot, the mobilization effect of hidden supporters seen in past presidential elections may have been relatively limited. 
 The defection of Republican voters, President Trump's core support base, is also drawing attention. 
 Charlie Cook, founder of the U.S. election analysis publication The Cook Political Report, previously defined this midterm election as a "unicorn election" differing in pattern from traditional contests, analyzing that the core variables are not moderates or independents, but traditional Republican voters disappointed with President Trump. 
 In particular, he pointed out that rural and small-town voters suffering economic hardships due to high oil prices, tariffs, trade wars, and the war in Iran are harboring dissatisfaction with President Trump's policy decisions. 
 He suggested that even if they do not cast ballots for Democratic candidates, they could express their dissatisfaction by staying home or skipping votes for Republican candidates. 
 Cook evaluated this phenomenon as closer to a "Red Undertow"—where enthusiasm among the Republican base weakens—rather than a "Blue Wave," which sees an explosive spread of Democratic support. 
 However, whether the Democrats' lead will translate into final results and what the margin of polling error was will likely only be accurately assessed after vote counting concludes in key battlegrounds. 
 Furthermore, the political significance of this election may vary depending on whether the Republicans' underperformance stems from a shift of votes toward the Democrats or a decline in voter turnout among the existing Republican base.
